title: Reflecting on reflecting
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino considers how teachers can reflect effectively on professional development and on their own lessons. She admits that self-evaluation forms after CPD often just match existing practice or yield intentions she never acts on. She argues that changing habits is hard and recommends small manageable changes aligned with the CPD undertaken. Reflection on lessons helps, particularly when the same topic is taught to several classes, but it can lead to wrong conclusions, as when she once used free time as a motivator. She lists what corrected her: observing colleagues, engaging with edu-Twitter, talking with teachers of shared classes, and discussing incidents with SLT and her head of department. She closes with a warning about overthinking and the value of reading and conversation.
points: Castelino notes that CPD reflection forms can degrade into restating existing habits or intentions that are never carried out.
She recommends small, manageable changes that align with CPD, because changing habits is difficult and unchanged habits stifle improvement.
She argues reflection can produce a wrong conclusion, as with free time as a motivator, so reflection needs external checks.
Her corrective practices include observing many teachers in detail, reading widely, jointly reflecting on shared classes and scripting responses with SLT.
She warns the line between reflecting and overthinking is thin, and that reading and conversation help reflection stay purposeful.
quotes: Usually, this has been in the form of a self-evaluation sheet guiding me to consider how and when I can use the CPD in my practice. I have to admit that when filling these forms, either I have written down something that I had already been doing and simply matched it to the CPD I was reflecting on, or I have written down something I genuinely wanted to try out but then didn’t for various reasons.

One of these reasons is that it is really hard to change habits. But keeping the same habits can make it harder for us to be effective teachers and can stifle our improvement, according to this eye-opening research by Hobbiss et al. So when it comes to CPD, it is important I remove any barriers so that I can committ to applying CPD to my practice. One way I can achieve this is by making small, manageable changes to my practice that are in line with CPD I undertake but that don’t radically change the way I teach.

Besides CPD, one of the most important ways to improve our practice is by reflecting on the lessons we teach. I find it so helpful when I teach the same topic to different classes in a year group. By the third time I have explained enzyme action in a week, the wording and the way I introduce examples and explanations are close to perfect (I am forever reflecting on how to improve further, which is why I don’t consider it perfect!).

But what if, following reflection of a lesson, I come to the wrong conclusion or, more realistically, a conclusion that is not exactly right? For example, when teaching a class, I may find that promising 5 minutes of ‘free time’ at the end of a lesson makes students work well. I reflect on this lesson and come to the conslusion that with this class, giving them free time is an excellent motivator, and I continue using this practice.
Reflecting is vital to improving our practice but there can be a fine line between reflecting and overthinking. I have certainly been guilty of the latter.

This is definitely applicable to teaching too! The more I read and the more conversations I have, the more I can effectively reflect with purpose. I may not get everything right each time, but thinking about why that is and relating it to past experience, other peoples’ experiences, and what the research says, can only serve to help.
